title: Sentence Foundations
description: Learn the building blocks of clear English sentences.

topics.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
topics.description: Match singular and plural subjects with the correct verb forms.
topics.definition: Subject–verb agreement means that the verb in a sentence must match its subject in number and person.
rules: Use a singular verb with a singular subject and a plural verb with a plural subject.
In the present simple, add -s or -es to the verb when the subject is he, she, or it.

examples.explanation: The singular subject 'student' takes the singular verb 'reads'.
The plural subject 'students' takes the plural verb 'read'.

topics.quickTip: Find the main subject first, then choose the verb form that matches it.

topics.title: Basic Sentence Structure
topics.description: Arrange subjects, verbs, and objects into complete sentences.
topics.definition: A basic English sentence expresses a complete thought and normally contains a subject followed by a verb, with an object or complement when needed.
rules: Place the subject before the verb in a standard statement.
Include an object after a transitive verb to show who or what receives the action.

examples.explanation: Maya is the subject, writes is the verb, and stories is the object.
The linking verb 'is' connects the subject to its complement.

topics.quickTip: Check that your sentence answers: who or what, does what, and—when needed—to whom or what.

topics.title: Independent and Dependent Clauses
topics.description: Recognize complete ideas and clauses that need more information.
topics.definition: An independent clause can stand alone as a complete sentence, while a dependent clause contains a subject and verb but cannot express a complete thought by itself.
rules: An independent clause must contain a subject, a verb, and a complete thought.
Connect a dependent clause to an independent clause to form a complete sentence.

examples.sentence: I stayed inside because it was raining.
examples.explanation: 'I stayed inside' is independent; 'because it was raining' is dependent.

examples.sentence: When the bell rang, the class ended.
examples.explanation: The opening dependent clause is completed by the independent clause.

commonMistakes.correct: I went to bed because I was tired.
We left when the meeting finished.

topics.quickTip: If a group of words begins with because, when, although, or if, check that it is joined to a complete thought.

title: Verbs and Time
description: Understand how verb forms communicate when actions happen.

topics.title: Present Simple
topics.description: Describe routines, habits, facts, and repeated actions.
topics.definition: The present simple describes habits, routines, general truths, and situations that are regularly or permanently true.
rules: Use the base verb with I, you, we, and they.
Add -s or -es to the verb with he, she, and it.

examples.explanation: This sentence describes a regular habit.
This sentence states a general truth.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I am go to class daily.

topics.quickTip: Words such as always, usually, often, and every day commonly signal the present simple.

topics.title: Past Simple
topics.description: Talk about completed actions and events in the past.
topics.definition: The past simple describes an action or situation that started and finished at a definite time in the past.
rules: Add -ed to regular verbs; learn the separate forms of irregular verbs.
Use did not plus the base verb for negatives and did plus the base verb for questions.

examples.explanation: The visit was completed at a stated past time.
'Wrote' is the irregular past form of 'write'.

topics.quickTip: After 'did' or 'did not', always use the base form of the main verb.

topics.title: Present Perfect
topics.description: Connect past actions and experiences to the present.
topics.definition: The present perfect links the past to the present and is formed with have or has plus the past participle.
rules: Use have with I, you, we, and they; use has with he, she, and it.
Use it for experiences or past actions with a present result when no finished past time is stated.

examples.sentence: I have visited Mumbai three times.
examples.explanation: This describes life experience without a finished time.
The past action has a present result: she does not have the keys now.

topics.quickTip: Use the past simple—not the present perfect—with finished-time words such as yesterday or last week.
